items.content:
RT @MsftSecIntel: On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, version 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served on the Cursor extension marketplace for a few hours. https://t.co/AOSQOdtjFU 

Microsoft has confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from the Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace extension and the npm anthropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected by this incident. 

Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace. At this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to the Cursor marketplace.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed the JavaScript embedded into the malicious extension package. The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details. 

Successful remote access depends on host privileges, SSH configuration, and the attacker’s server configuration; however, the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails.

Read the blog for technical analysis and guidance on identifying affected systems, investigating endpoint and network activity, and removing confirmed malicious SSH keys and persistence artifacts.

items.content:
RT @spycraft101: Stanford University student Elsa Johnson became a target of the Chinese Communist Party in 2024.

Elsa attended a private school as a child with a heavy focus on foreign languages and became fluent in Mandarin Chinese while still in elementary school. Years later after she was accepted to Stanford, she studied international relations and researched Chinese industry and military tactics while working at the Hoover Institution on campus.

She soon came to the attention of members of the Chinese Communist Party, which has a heavy presence at Stanford and throughout Southern California. There are currently more than 1,000 Chinese students attending Stanford each year, and the university has received more than $64,000,000 in private donations from Chinese individuals and organizations since 2010.

In June 2024, a man claiming to be a fellow Stanford student named Charles Chen contacted her online. She was not initially suspicious as they had many mutual associates, and his photos and posts appeared to be centered on campus. But his questions and requests quickly put her on edge as he invited her on a paid trip to China. And he seemingly knew details about her that she had never shared with him.

When she tried to disengage with him, she began receiving threatening phone calls by Chinese speakers. Elsa contacted Stanford administrators and the FBI, who told her Charles was likely affiliated with the Ministry of State Security, had been posing as a Stanford student for years, and had targeted at least ten other female students since 2020 in a similar manner. They also told her she was under physical surveillance on campus by the Chinese Communist Party.

Elsa wrote articles in the Stanford Review and The Free Press about Chinese influence on campus, and in March 2026 testified about espionage threats on college campuses before the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
For episode 270 of the Spycraft 101 podcast I spoke with Elsa about being targeted by a foreign government right in the middle of a US college campus. The episode is available now.

items.content:
RT @Hannibal9972485: Binance 🚨🚨is  balance sheet restructuring & trying to stop a  bank run that was likely already forming due to their internal bad debts or fractional reserve practices. .  Binance is facing a massive liquidity crisis (maybe due to bad loans, FTX-style internal trading desk losses, or regulatory freezes). They need to lock up $6.3 billion in user funds without admitting insolvency. 🚨
They engineered a "hack" using the EIP-7702 vector. They move the funds to wallets they control. They freeze $3B of it (to stop the bank run on their own exchange) and let $3.3B "escape" into dormant BTC wallets and Uniswap swaps (which are likely wash trades back to their own market makers). They crash the market 4-5% to liquidate short positions and scoop up cheap assets.
🚨
Look at the forensic breakdown of the attack. In the span of 20 minutes, the attacker drained funds across ten different blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, XRP, Optimism, and Avalanche.
🚨
These blockchains do not share the same cryptographic curves or key types. Bitcoin uses ECDSA (secp256k1). Solana uses Ed25519. XRP uses its own variant of ECDSA. A single compromised laptop does not possess the magical ability to sign valid transactions across ten fundamentally different cryptographic architectures in 20 minutes. As TRM Labs explicitly noted in the forensic data, a single phished Ethereum authorization cannot explain Bitcoin, Tron, XRP Ledger, Solana, and layer-2 transfers all occurring simultaneously
🚨
If a real hacker compromised their laptop, they would have to navigate Binance’s internal infrastructure to access 10 separate, isolated hot-wallet signing services, bypassing hardware security modules and multisig requirements for each individual chain. That takes hours or days of lateral movement, not 20 minutes.
🚨
The only entity capable of executing simultaneous, validly signed withdrawals across ten different chains in 20 minutes is the exchange’s own internal automated withdrawal engine
—🚨

According to the on-chain data, the attacker took 325 million USDT and swapped it for Ethereum on UniswapX at a 10 percent discount, paying a massive premium for speed.

Professional market makers absorbed that trade. Why would an external hacker take a 10 % haircut on an irreversible, unsanctioned swap when they control the wallet? They wouldn't.⚠️⚠️🚨

Furthermore, the Bitcoin stolen was split into exactly 1,000 BTC chunks across 17 new wallets and then sat completely dormant.
🚨
It was not laundered. It was not moved to a mixer. It was organized into clean, institutional-sized blocks and parked. Hackers do not park stolen funds in neat, 1,000 BTC increments. Institutional custodians do this when they are restructuring balance sheets or moving funds to cold storage under their own control.🚨

The attacker even routed test transactions back to itself before the main sweep.

This is the behavior of an internal engineer testing a deployment script.🚨
—-

Binance is doing exactly what FTX did before its collapse, just with a more sophisticated smokescreen. They have halted withdrawals. They are promising to make users whole with money they do not have.
🚨
Within the next 30 to 60 days, Binance will slowly resume withdrawals for small retail users to maintain the illusion of solvency. Large institutional whales will find their accounts frozen indefinitely pending "investigation" into the hacked funds. The $3.3 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum currently sitting in dormant wallets will not be recovered. It will be slowly commingled with other exchange flows over the next year to quietly plug Binance's internal holes.
🚨
You are watching a bank robbery designed to hide the fact that the largest exchange on earth is out of money.

items.content:
regarding cve-2026-98432: it is a uaf in tcp, mptcp is needed to make the race win and to get the leak and write.

the impact of the bug is bad, its essentially go2shell, caddy2shell etc. go 1.24+ servers are all vulnerable, because mptcp  is enabled by default.

BUT:

1. It is extremely hard to win the race reliably, anthropic said it took 40 mins for them to get leak and defeat kaslr 
2. It is probably hard to exploit in practice. most routers, lbs and isps drop ip options, without that header you can't race at all, so realistically only a same network attacker can try, which is pretty common in sandbox infra

my mythos worked on this for last 3 days burned ~$2k and couldn't build a reliable poc that can be sprayable. gpt-5.6 sol als exhausted my subscription and couldn't even get a leak. 

either anthropic has a unreleased model which is better than their public one or they have a pro exploit dev internally.

items.content:
RT @DarkWebInformer: 🚨 Critical Linux kernel TCP flaw enables remote root code execution; CVE-2026-98432

A race condition in the Linux kernel’s IPv4 TCP implementation can trigger a use-after-free before application authentication, potentially allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to leak kernel memory, corrupt memory or crash the system.

Anthropic says Claude developed a working exploit that executed attacker-chosen commands as root against Linux servers with a Multipath TCP listener. The exploit took approximately 53 minutes to complete during testing and has not been publicly released.
⠀
• CVSS: 9.8 Critical, according to the Linux kernel CVE team
• Affected: Linux kernels beginning with version 4.4
• Fixed: 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3
• Attack requirements: Network access, no credentials and no user interaction
• Exploitation status: No known attacks in the wild
⠀
Ubuntu and Red Hat Enterprise Linux had not released corrected kernel packages as of October 29. Debian, Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux and SUSE have released fixes for at least some affected branches.

Distribution severity ratings differ substantially. Red Hat rates the flaw 5.9 because it considers the race difficult to win and describes denial of service as the most likely practical impact.
items.author: 0xocdsec

items.content:
RT @derekmross: 🚨 PSA for anyone running a Linux server, node, or relay

CVE-2026-98432 is a critical Linux kernel bug (CVSS 9.8). Someone on the internet can send crafted TCP packets and take over your machine. No login needed.

Ubuntu and Red Hat haven't shipped a fixed kernel yet. Debian, SUSE, Oracle and Amazon have.

What to do today:

1. Check your kernel: uname -r
Fixed versions: 6.1.190+, 6.6.159+, 6.12.113+, 6.18.56+, 7.2.10+ or 7.3+. Below that, you're exposed.

2. If your distro has a fix, update and reboot.

3. If not, block the attack. It needs TCP packets with "IP options," which normal traffic never uses. One nftables rule drops them. Log what gets dropped so you can see if someone's probing you.

4. Turn off MPTCP unless you need it:
sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0
Programs built with Go 1.24+ use MPTCP automatically, and that's how the known exploit gets in.

5. Make it survive a reboot, and check it still works after one.

If you run a Bitcoin node, a Lightning node or a Nostr relay, your machine is on the internet by design. Do this today.

Self-hosting is freedom. Patching is part of the job. 🛡️

items.content:
RT @r0ckstardev: 🔴 If you have a VM running Ubuntu and want to patch the CVE-2026-98432 Critical Linux Kernel Flaw, here is the script I used to secure my servers:

# CVE-2026-98432 stopgap. For Ubuntu 20.04 and 24.04.
# Log in as ubuntu, copy everything in this file, paste it into the SSH session.
# Done when the last line prints: active
sudo apt-get update -qq </dev/null && sudo apt-get install -y nftables </dev/null
sudo tee /etc/nftables-cve-2026-98432.nft >/dev/null <<'EOF'
add table inet cve_2026_98432
flush table inet cve_2026_98432
table inet cve_2026_98432 {
chain pre {
type filter hook prerouting priority raw - 10; policy accept;
ip hdrlength > 5 meta l4proto tcp counter drop
}
}
EOF
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/cve-2026-98432-nft.service >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=CVE-2026-98432 stopgap: drop IPv4 TCP with IP options
After=https://t.co/yv6n00FLOm
Before=https://t.co/w7O0ZyUiWr docker.service
[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=yes
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/nft -f /etc/nftables-cve-2026-98432.nft
[Install]
WantedBy=https://t.co/XN4fnfddjw
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now cve-2026-98432-nft.service && systemctl is-active cve-2026-98432-nft.service

RT @r0ckstardev: I spent the last few hours going down the CVE-2026-98432 Critical Linux Kernel Flaw rabbit hole 🕳️ and here are a few thoughts:

- It is legit and scary. Kinda crazy that it's been known for 2 weeks & there is still no patch for popular distros (the Ubuntu fix, for example, is developed but not publicly released, still in testing).
- MPTCP needs to be enabled, and on some unorthodox port. It seems that ISPs globally have started blocking options on 22, 80, 443 and other popular ports (good!).

- It takes about 50 minutes on average to gain access to a server if all conditions are met. My servers started getting hit today; luckily the script I shared earlier handled the situation and rejected the probes.

Stay safe & enjoy the wild AI psychosis ride we're in.

items.content:
RT @TrevorCampbell_: Just got a phishing email that Gmail authenticated as Google. DKIM/DMARC passed. I can see a lot of people falling for this one, since it plays to the idea that your account has already been compromised.

Scammer puts the scam in an app-password name, triggers a real Google alert, then forwards the alert email to your email address.

How this attack works, and why it’s convincing:

1. The trick: The attacker puts the threatening text and shortened URL into an app password’s customizable name on another account. Google incorporates that text into a real security notification and signs the email.

2. The delivery: That notification is forwarded through another mailbox to the victim. In this message, Gmail still recorded passing Google DKIM and DMARC authentication.

3. What makes it convincing: The Google sender, signature, branding, and “Check activity” button are legitimate. The suspected attacker-supplied text appears inside the same trusted-looking template, using a deadline to push you toward its separate link.

4. The giveaway: Both the notification and its genuine Google button refer to someone else’s account. The “permanent access after 24 hours” claim is false; app passwords can be revoked.

Be careful out there folks!

items.content:
Drunken Korean bar rant: 

Perhaps the most important takeaway from @unpromptedsf is the widening disconnect between demonstrated AI capability & the narrative being constructed around it.

Frontier AI labs & their financial backers have a vested interest in weaponizing the credibility of exceptional researchers, turning legitimate breakthroughs into the perception that AI possesses capabilities it has yet to reliably demonstrate. Fear, hype, & the promise of technological superiority are powerful instruments for shaping public perception, influencing markets, & attracting investment.

Yet much of this impressive research remains fundamentally dependent on years of human expertise, technical intuition, & highly specialized domain knowledge. These are not incidental contributions. They are often the very reason these breakthroughs are possible in the 1st place.

The work coming out of labs like @calif_io is a perfect textbook example. Their research deserves genuine recognition & respect. Many of the people behind it are figures I have admired for years, as have countless others in our industry. That admiration, however, should not exempt the commercial interests funding & promoting their work from scrutiny. Their motivations, incentives, and ultimate objectives deserve far more attention.

We should be able to celebrate meaningful advances in AI without allowing frontier labs to repackage exceptional human achievement as evidence of autonomous machine capability. Recognizing the value of AI should never require diminishing the expertise of the researchers making these advances possible.

There is a fundamental difference between advancing science and manufacturing the perception of progress. Increasingly, the latter appears to be the more lucrative business.

What concerns me most is how effectively this narrative has drawn some of our industry's most respected figures into its orbit, lending their hard-earned credibility to a marketing machine whose interests may not necessarily align with their own.

And judging by the public reaction, it's working remarkably well... Sadly

RT @PabloSabbatella: 27 - Download the security tools from @objective_see see for MacOS. They are OpenSource and free, developed by @patrickwardle .
- Lulu is a firewall that will protect you from incoming attacks and will stop malware from exfiltrating data if you get infected.
- Knock Knock and BlockBlock protect you from persistent software
- TaskExplorer analyzes all processes running, their signatures and checks with VirusTotal if they are infected.
- ReiKey checks if some process is checking your keystrokes (keyloggers)
- DoNotDisturb alerts if someone opened the lid from your Mac, takes a picture and sends it through Telegram
